translations.text: Concerning them the prophet said through God's Spirit, "I will send my fishers, and they will fish for them; and my hunters, and they will hunt them from every mountain and from every hill."
Afterwards he chose the wealthy. But if he had not first chosen the poor, it would have seemed to the wealthy that they had been chosen for their possessions.
Now he sits in heaven, clothed in the human nature that he took on in this life. He urges us to turn to him, so that we always cleanse our ways of sins and correct them according to his commandments.
But in this matter we should consider their desire more than their wealth. Whoever keeps nothing for himself gives up a great deal.
Peter and Andrew gave up a great deal when each of them completely gave up the wish to own things and renounced his own desires.
Now someone says, "I would like to imitate the apostles, who scorned all worldly things, but I have no possessions to give up."
See: these holy merchants, Peter and Andrew, bought eternal life for themselves with their nets and their boat.
The kingdom of God has no fixed price. It is valued according to what a person has.

The kingdom of heaven was given to these brothers we have mentioned in return for their net and boat. Later it was given to the rich man Zacchaeus for half of his possessions, to a certain widow for a farthing, and to a certain man for a drink of water.
Then Christ looked up at the rich man and said, "Zacchaeus, come down quickly, because today I must stay at your house."
Then the Lord said to his disciples, "I tell you truly, this poor widow has brought a greater offering than any of these rich men."
In our language this means, "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will." No offering pleases God as much as good will does.
About this the psalmist said, "In me sunt, Deus, vota tua, quae reddam laudationes tibi": "Almighty God, your vows are upon me, and I will repay them to you with praises."
For you do not live on our gifts. Instead, you are more delighted by the offering of our heart.
For this reason the holy preachers would not covet anything in this world with greed, nor have any private possessions, so that they could love one another deeply, without envy.
Truly, the prophet Isaiah foresaw these apostles who were to come, when he said through God's Spirit, "Who are these who fly here like clouds, and like doves to their windows?"
The prophet saw them despise earthly possessions, draw near to heaven with their minds, abound in the words of life and shine with miracles, and he called them doves and flying clouds.
Our windows are our eyes, through which our soul looks at whatever it desires outside. The dove is a gentle creature, free from the bitterness of gall.
Truly the holy apostles were like doves at their windows, since they desired nothing in this world,
but looked upon all things innocently, and were not drawn by any eagerness for plunder toward what they saw outside.
He who desires through plunder the things that he sees outside with his eyes is a kite, not a dove at his windows.
We have now gone through part of the commentary on this gospel. Now we will tell you the meaning of the names of the four apostles whom Christ chose at the beginning.

Simon is interpreted as 'obedient,' and Peter as 'acknowledging,' Andrew as 'manly'; James is called 'supplanter,' and John 'God's grace.' Every Christian should keep the meaning of these names fully in his way of life.

Peter was called Simon before his conversion, but Christ named him Peter, which means 'acknowledging,' because he acknowledged Christ with true faith when he said, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God."
Without doubt, whoever rightly acknowledges God and obeys him keeps the meaning of these two names in his way of life.
If he bears hardship manfully for God's name, and resists the devil's temptations like a man, then he fulfils in his conduct the meaning of Andrew, which is interpreted as 'manly.'
James is called 'supplanter,' and he is a true supplanter who wisely supplants his fleshly sins and the devil's enticement.
John is called 'God's grace.' He is fittingly called God's grace who through good merits obtains God's grace, so that he may zealously fulfil his commandments.
After Christ's passion, the apostle Andrew went to the land called Achaia. There he preached faith in the Lord and the redemption of the world through his passion.
Then Aegeas, a cruel judge, wanted to stamp out his preaching and force the Christians into devilish worship.

Andrew said to him, "Since you are a judge of men, it would befit you to acknowledge your own Judge, who is in heaven, and to worship him who is the true God, and turn your mind away from the false gods."
Aegeas answered him, "Are you Andrew, who overthrows the temples of our gods and incites this people to the vain teaching that the Roman rulers have rejected and ordered to be stamped out?"
Andrew answered him, "The Roman rulers have not yet acknowledged God's truth: how the Son of God came to men and taught that these idols
that you worship are not gods at all, but are the worst devils, enemies of mankind, who teach men how to anger Almighty God,
"And then he abandons them, and the devil mocks them until they leave their bodies guilty and naked, taking nothing with them except their sins."
Aegeas said, "These are empty words. Indeed, when your Saviour preached these words, the Jews fastened him to the gallows of the cross."

Andrew answered him, "Oh, if only you would understand the mystery of the holy cross! With what wise love the Lord of mankind accepted the gallows of the cross to restore us, not because he was forced to, but of his own free will."
Andrew answered, "I said 'of his own free will' because I was with him when he was betrayed by his disciple, and before his passion he told us in advance,
and that he would rise from death on the third day. He said that he had power to lay down his soul, and power to take it up again."
Egeas said, "I wonder at you, a wise man, that you are willing to follow this teaching, however it came about, willingly or by force, that he was fastened on a cross."
Andrew answered him, "Great is the mystery of the cross, which I will reveal to you, if you are willing to hear me." Egeas said, "It cannot truly be called a mystery, but a punishment."
Andrew said, "You will see that this very punishment is the mystery of mankind's renewal, if you are willing to hear me patiently."
Egeas answered, "I will hear you patiently, but if you do not obey me, you shall receive the same mystery of the cross on yourself."
Andrew answered him, "If I feared the gallows of the cross, I would not preach the glory of the cross."
Aegeas said, "Your senseless talk preaches the punishment of the cross as a glory, because in your boldness you do not fear the punishment of death."
Andrew answered, "Not out of presumption but out of faith, I do not fear the torment of death. The death of righteous men is precious, and the death of sinful men is wretched."
Egeas said, "Unless you offer sacrifice to our almighty gods, I will order you to be tormented and fastened on the same cross that you praise."
Andrew said to him, "Every day I offer my sacrifice to Almighty God, who alone is the true God.
Not the flesh of lowing bulls or the blood of goats; instead, every day I offer the spotless Lamb on the altar of the holy cross,
and it remains whole and alive after all the people eat its flesh and drink its blood." Egeas asked, "How can that be so?"
Andrew answered him, "If you wish to learn how that can be, then take on the form of a disciple, so that you may learn these mysteries."
Egeas said, "I will get the understanding of this matter out of you by torture."
The holy apostle answered, "I wonder greatly at you, how you have turned to such great folly that you think I will reveal the divine mysteries to you because of torture.
You have heard the mystery of the holy offering. Now, if you believe that Christ, the Son of God, who was hanged on the cross, is true God,
then I will reveal to you how the Lamb remains whole and unblemished in his kingdom after it is offered, and its flesh eaten, and its blood drunk.
But if you will not believe, you will never come to insight into this truth."
So then Egeas grew angry, and ordered the apostle to be thrust into a dark prison.
Then a great crowd from the whole province came to the prison. They wanted to kill Aegeas and lead the apostle out of the prison.
Then Andrew said to all the multitude, "My brothers, do not stir the gentle Lord to any anger by what you are attempting.
Our Saviour was betrayed, and he was patient: he did not quarrel or cry out, nor did anyone hear his voice in the streets.

Keep quiet and peace now, and do not hinder my martyrdom, but rather prepare yourselves as God's soldiers, so that with fearless minds you may overcome all threats and bodily torments through patience.
If any terror is to be feared, then it is the one that has no end. Truly, the fear of man is like smoke, which vanishes quickly when it is stirred.
The pains in this world are either light and bearable, or they are heavy and quickly drive the soul out.

The pains that are prepared for the wicked in the world to come are eternal. There is weeping every day, and wailing, and lamentation, and endless torment, and Egeas is hastening there without hesitation."
Be all the more ready for this, so that through passing affliction you may come to the eternal joys, where you will always rejoice, flourishing and reigning with Christ."
When the apostle had taught the people such words all through the night, at dawn Egeas sent to the prison and ordered the holy apostle to be brought to him, and said,

There is no city left in all this land in which the temples of our gods have not been abandoned. Now the worship of our gods must be restored again through you, so that they may be gladdened by you and you may be in our friendship.
Until now I have spoken to you gently, so that you might acknowledge the true faith through reason. But now you persist in your shamelessness and think that I ought to be afraid of your threats.
Then the Christian people ran toward the executioners who were leading him to the cross, crying out and saying, "What has this righteous man and friend of God done to deserve crucifixion?"
Then they came up, raised him onto the cross, and bound his whole body with stiff cords, just as they had been commanded.
More than twenty thousand people stood there with Egeas's brother, crying out together, "It is an unjust judgement that this holy man should suffer like this."

Truly, from the cross the holy Andrew strengthened the hearts of the faithful people, urging them to patience in this passing life and saying that this short suffering is not to be compared with the eternal reward.
Meanwhile all the people went to Egeas's residence, all crying out together and saying that so holy a man should not hang there;
a virtuous man, adorned with good conduct, a noble teacher, merciful and kind, wise and pure, ought not to suffer like this, but ought to be released from the cross while still alive;
for he does not stop preaching the truth, though he has now hung there alive for two days.
So Egeas feared the crowd, promised that he would release him as they wished, and went along with them.
When the apostle saw him, he asked, "Well now, Egeas, why have you come to us?
If you are still willing to believe in the Saviour, you will be shown mercy, as I promised you.
If you have come in order to release me, I do not wish to be released from here alive. Now I clearly see my true King; I stand in his sight, praying to him.
I pity you and your misery, for eternal damnation awaits you.
Hurry now, wretched man, while you are still able to do anything, so that you do not end up wanting to when it is denied you."
Then they tried to release him, but the hands of anyone who touched the cross grew stiff.
Then the apostle cried out to the Saviour Christ in a very loud voice, praying like this: "My good Master, do not let me be released unless you first receive my spirit."
After these words a great light was seen coming suddenly from heaven to the apostle. It shone all around him, so that human eyes could not see him because of the heavenly light that surrounded him.
The light remained for nearly an hour, and Andrew gave up his spirit in that light and went to Christ together with the radiance. To Christ be glory for ever throughout all the world.
On the way home, before he reached his house, Egeas was seized by a horrible devil. He went utterly mad and was thrown to the ground in the sight of the people who were walking with him.
So the cruel man departed from the world to hell. His brother kept the body of the holy Andrew with great reverence, so that he might escape [Egeas's fate].
Such great fear spread over all the people that no one was left there who did not believe in God.
The priests and deacons of that people, who saw it all, wrote down this passion, so that no one would doubt this account.
Let us now pray to the Almighty Ruler that his blessed apostle may be our intercessor, just as he was the herald of his Church.
To the Creator Lord be honour and praise for ever and ever. Amen, we say.
